The RLM method is one of the more interesting ideas in the last 6 months or so. It’s taken a while to see any concrete implementations of it but they’re starting to emerge.

The @inference_net team is really pushing it forward with HALO one of the first truly useful implementations of the method. In addition to the core they’ve implemented some interesting things on their cloud and just added a desktop app. Note: imo HALO was a bit of a game changer in the eval space.

Another interesting implementation was LCM (Long Context Management) which uses RLM more as inspiration than exact implementation but the idea caught my attention. Sadly unlike HALO’s constant iteration LCM seems to have been a one and done experiment. 

There’s also fast-rlm which looks intriguing with its ACP support. 
https://t.co/OhwaYwUq8d

These are all very different expressions of the RLM paper and I’m really looking to more work based on it. 

As for myself I’d love to have the time to pick up where LCM left off and see where it could go. It had so much potential.

This is why "forex gurus" sell you a course instead of encouraging you to study institutional finance and understand how interbank liquidity actually works.

If the students of Habby Forex and Jeffrey Benson truly understood capital dynamics, they would never believe the ridiculous claim that Jeffrey withdrew $9 million from an offshore retail broker like Assex Markets or Kwakol. The only way such a massive withdrawal could legitimately happen is if these brokers possessed active clearing contracts and institutional settlement lines with Tier-1 liquidity providers like JPMorgan Chase, which they simply do not have.

The primary purpose of selling courses is to control the narrative and keep students in the dark. The irony is that, strictly speaking, these influencers are not even real forex traders, and their audience fails to realize this due to a complete misunderstanding of market microstructure and broker execution models.

A retail broker like the ones Habby Forex promotes is no different from a Bet9ja shop. When you walk into Bet9ja and place a bet that Real Madrid will beat Barcelona, you are simply entering into a private wager with the betting house. 
Real Madrid, Barcelona, and La Liga have no idea your bet exists, and neither the players nor the league earn anything whether you win or lose. Your win is an outright loss for the betting house, and your loss is their direct profit. The betting house remains profitable because they know that over 90% of gamblers will eventually lose all their money, and even the rare few who win substantial sums usually gamble it all back.

This is precisely how the brokers used by Habby Forex and Jeffrey Benson operate. When you open their trading app, you see live charts of forex price movements, much like watching live scores on a sports betting app. But when you place an order, that trade is logged solely on the broker's private server. The broker makes zero attempt to route or execute your order in the real interbank market. Routing orders to real global liquidity providers requires massive upfront capital, bridge fees, and transaction costs. Because statistics show that roughly 90% of retail traders wipe out their account balance within 90 days, the broker has no financial incentive to incur costs by sending your order to the real market. They simply wait for you to blow your account so they can pocket 100% of your deposit.

This is also why these brokers offer absurd leverage like 1:2000, as it ensures you lose your money as quickly as possible. In the real financial world, leverage consists of strictly collateralized credit lines. In the United States, retail leverage is legally capped at 1:50; in the UK and EU, it is capped at 1:30; and in many emerging markets, it is even lower to prevent systemic risk due to lack of liquidity.

Ultimately, these brokers partner with forex influencers like Habby and Jeffrey Benson to funnel inexperienced traders onto their platforms. They pay these influencers massive commissions for every referral, and under certain affiliate deals, they even pay them a percentage of their followers' trading losses, because client losses are where the broker makes the most money.

If you're making software that is designed to parse complex, diverse data, especially when YOU don't control the data, and it is generated in varied ways by thousands of different organizations or users, then there's really no substitute for what's known as "fuzzing" tests.

Fuzzing is a testing technique where you try to intelligently generate a huge number of varied inputs to your program, with the goal of finding parsing bugs that you'd be unlikely to come across if you're only testing with a fixed set of valid inputs.

A naive approach to generating random inputs would be wasteful, since most inputs are trivially invalid and can be quickly rejected.

What you really want are inputs that are pathological; ones that are nearly valid but have some bizarre issue that can confuse your parsing rules and trigger code pathways that you'd normally never traverse.

Fuzzing used to be a somewhat esoteric approach used by security-focused engineers in high-stakes, sophisticated applications. But now anyone can use it. I have a skill specifically for fuzzing you can try here:

https://t.co/4GXFLCYvWD

It's part of a series of testing-related skills that also includes metamorphic testing, conformance harness testing, golden artifact generation, end-to-end integration testing, etc. 

The skill works across many popular languages and automatically installs the needed tooling for you, instruments your application for fuzzing, and then mounts extended fuzz testing campaigns. 

You can see an example of one in the screenshot, where it's been working for many hours, subjecting three different parsers in my hedge_fund_data_tool to torture tests. 

For instance, my elaborate parser for SEC insider trade forms (i.e., Forms 3, 4, and 5), which is thousands of lines of Rust, has been called over 780 million times, each invocation with a different, optimally selected input designed to best explore all the different possible code paths within the parser.

There aren't that many forms of this kind in the history of the SEC's EDGAR database, across all companies. The only way to do something like that is with fuzzing. And now you can!

More and more, I’m realizing that the use of external library dependencies in Rust projects is an anti-pattern. 

Most libraries are one-size-fits-all, with scope creep and sprawling dependency chains that lead to you depending on hundreds of different projects and people, any one of which could suffer from a supply-chain attack.

They also often rely on C or C++ libraries, which defeats the benefit of the strict memory safety that is the major selling point of Rust. This usually results in complex and annoying build processes that create headaches when you want everything to be cross-platform.

And even when they don’t use C or C++ libraries, they almost always make liberal use of unsafe code. If you don’t make strict memory safety a basic requirement, it’s easy to slip into bad patterns out of convenience or a sense of misguided pragmatism.

Perhaps worst of all, they are just not performance-optimized the way things can and should be today, with special tricks to optimize performance specifically on Apple silicon or on high-core-count AMD processors. 

Those two platforms have very different performance characteristics and need specialized designs to even approach the point of saturating the hardware.

For my FrankenSearch project, which is the core of my cass tool and also used in various other projects of mine like agent mail and eidetic engine, I have been using the Tantivy library for fast lexical search. 

Tantivy is sort of a Rust descendant of Lucene, which is the core search system used in Elasticsearch. 

I realized recently that many of the things that annoy me about FrankenSearch come from Tantivy, and I hate the feeling that it’s a walled-off dependency that I don’t want to change for the obvious reasons. 

Since for my newest projects (e.g., FrankenOCR, FrankenMarkdown, FrankenSim, and FrankenGraphDB), I have a strict “no outside dependencies” rule other than my own projects like Asupersync and FrankenSQLite, I decided that I should start applying a similar standard in my older projects. 

That’s why I decided to create my own specialized lexical search system optimized specifically for FrankenSearch. I’ve made the plan for it and the implementation work is already far along. You can see the plan here:

https://t.co/8PHIpapyOU

This will reduce the number of dependencies by 41 crates, increase safety and security, and dramatically increase performance. 

And because this module will be part of the core code of the system, it will benefit along with the rest of the projects from my endless continuous performance optimization campaigns, so it will keep getting faster and faster.

As the plan explains, the biggest wins come from not paying the “generality tax.” By not trying to be all things to all people, we can do just what we need in the absolute optimal way possible.

非洲真的很缺水吗？其实“懒”才是他们穷的根本原因。有数据显示，非洲地下水储量是地表的100倍，为何他们不挖井，而是到处找水？
我之前跟着一支海外工程队在那边待了快八个月，亲眼见过太多让人匪夷所思的事，说出来真的好多人都不敢信。我们当时的营地建在一片开阔的草地上，刚过去的时候要解决用水问题，队里找了个测水的师傅随便找了个地方打井，打到不到十二米就出了清水，水质甜得很，除了供我们队四十多个人吃喝洗澡，还能引出一垄水浇我们开出来的小菜园，天天浇水都用不完。
而离我们营地不到两公里的地方，就有一个百十来口人的部落村子，我第一次跟着采购去村里的时候，就看见全村人都围着一个半米深的泥坑接水，那水浑得放半小时都澄清不了，水面上还飘着虫子和牲畜的粪便，小孩渴了蹲下来直接舀了就喝，大人也不管，不少小孩隔三差五就拉肚子，缺药耽误着能拖出大病，看着真的让人心疼。我当时就问翻译，咱们这边打井出了这么多水，他们咋不来打一口？翻译笑笑说，你往后看就知道了，不是水的事。
没过多久工程闲下来，队长说反正咱们设备人都有，不如免费帮他们打一口井，也算做件好事，结果第一步就卡壳了。村长带着一群人堵在我们选好的井址，说这块地是他们部落的公用土地，要打井就得给他们十袋面粉五桶食用油外加两箱汽水，不然别想动土。我们队里想着反正也不多，给就给了，就当换一口井给村里人用，这点东西对我们来说不算什么。
接下来要找几个当地人帮忙打下手搬东西，我们说好一天给一斤玉米面两瓶汽水，这个待遇在当地已经够一个三口之家吃饱喝足了，比他们自己瞎晃赚得多太多，结果来了五个人，干了不到四十分钟，全都撂挑子坐到树底下乘凉去了，说太阳太晒，会晒伤皮肤，祖宗规矩就是正午不能干活，要等太阳落山再干活。我们想着入乡随俗那就等，结果太阳落山之后，连个人影都没见着，第二天上午好不容易来了三个，还要求必须先给汽水玉米面，不给就不动手，我们给了之后，三个人晃悠着挖了不到半米，又坐下来歇着聊天了，一聊就是一上午，第三天干脆全都不来了，托人带话来说拿到的吃的够喝够吃好几天，先回家休息，吃完了再来。
最后没办法，我们工程队自己上手，不到十天就打出了一口出水稳定的井，还给他们在井口安了简易的提水架，放了两个大木桶，跟村长说以后大家随便来打水，只要别往井里扔垃圾就行。一开始村里人可开心了，天天排着队来打水，结果半个月不到，井口就堵了，我们过去一看，大大小小的树枝石头烂叶子堵了小半井，原来大家打完水垃圾随手就扔在井口边上，下雨一冲全进去了。我们免费帮他们清干净，反复跟村长和村民说不要扔垃圾，要保持井口干净，结果不到两个月，又堵了，之后村长干脆来找我们，说井坏了，你们再帮我们打一口新的吧，那语气说得理所当然，好像我们就该天天给他们收拾烂摊子。
我之前还碰到过一次，营地的围墙坏了一段，找了四个当地工人来修，说好一天干完给对应的工钱，结果四个工人八点开工，九点就歇着喝茶，十点吃早饭，十二点要睡午觉，睡到下午三点才起来，干了不到一小时又说要回家喂孩子，一天下来只码了不到五块砖，第二天还过来要全额工钱，说我们没给他们提供茶和饼，所以干得慢，钱不能少给，当时给我们队长气得直接把他们赶走了。
待得久了我才发现，这种事真的不是个例。有个二十多岁的小伙子天天来我们营地卖野果，我们看他挺活络，就说你干脆天天给我们营地送菜，我们一个月给你固定的工钱，比你卖野果稳定多了，结果他干了三天，第四天就不见了，过了一周晃悠过来，问他为啥不来，他说前三天赚的钱够花了，在家歇着花完了再来。还有国际援助组织免费给他们发蔬菜种子，教他们开荒种地，说种好了够全村吃大半年，结果一半种子被他们煮着吃了，剩下的随便往地里一撒，既不浇水也不除草，长不出来就接着等着发援助。
真的，很多人说非洲穷是因为气候不好历史遗留问题，可我们明明看到脚底下十几米就是清水，储量够整个村子用几十年，有人免费帮你打出来，就只要随手维护一下都做不到。他们不是没有力气，跑出去找野果跳篝火舞能折腾一整天，一说到干活赚饭吃，半小时就喊累；也不是没有资源，地下水摆在那，援助摆在那，就是不肯伸手去动。
我待了八个月见过好多口废弃的援助井，全都是打完没两年没人维护废了，当地人宁愿背着水桶走三四公里去接脏雨水，也不肯花半天时间清一清堵了的井口。你说这到底是延续了几千年的靠天吃饭的生活方式已经刻进骨子里改不了，还是真的就是“懒”才导致一直摆脱不了穷呢？你怎么看这件事？

BOOM! Well, I'll be damned if that's not the very BEST-sounding, 100% simulated/synthesized concert grand piano I've ever heard!

https://t.co/iu5sbvEJ6I

What does that mean? ZERO recordings of real-world sounds were used (other than for comparison and diagnosis), nor were any measurements captured by microphones or similar.

Literally everything from start to finish here was part of an enormously intricate physics simulation of a piano: its geometry, materials, moving parts, and acoustic radiation.

Oh, and I did the same thing for a full drum kit and cymbals. The cymbals are modelled using the estimated geometry and dimpling pattern of a real Zildjian splash cymbal, together with estimated profile details and literature-based properties for B20 bronze alloy.

For the most extreme audio quality, you can pre-render to WAV files or similar. But after many, many rounds of iterative performance optimization, I now have the wasm version running at better than real-time, so it sounds really good live in the browser as well!

This is a big deal. It's shockingly hard to get truly realistic-sounding audio from synthesized instruments. The real world is just too complicated. What people usually end up doing is spending hundreds or thousands of dollars to buy these massive libraries of recorded sounds of a real piano, which takes up many gigs of space and is super slow to use.

The worst part of that approach isn't the size of the files, the cost of the sample packs, or the inelegance of the approach. It's that EVEN THAT is a massive simplification, because they are recording each key separately at various key velocities and so forth.

That means they are missing the very complex interaction effects that arise in a real piano when you play certain keys at the same time or after one another. The energy persists in the instrument and conditions the next sounds.

It's subtle but real and you pick up on it when it's missing. And yes, they do try to capture some of this, but they use very lossy methods with more simplified approximations that are way more primitive than what I'm doing here with FrankenSim.

I've invested a massive amount of time and focus on ensuring that the energy accounting is correct in these simulations.

And the same thing goes for drums! There are complex interaction effects. These sorts of things are emergent and "just fall out" when everything is simulated for REAL using the actual underlying physics.

So why haven't other companies and people done this? I'm not actually sure; it's kind of insane when you consider all those people working at Yamaha, Roland, Korg, Moog, etc. But my guess is that it's because it's super hard and complicated to get all the physics right and to program it the right way so that it's tractable without needing crazy amounts of compute.

Anyway, take a look at this demo site I set up. It's a lot of fun to play with, and at the bottom there is a nifty MIDI player that takes any MIDI file and lets you listen to it with the high-quality simulated piano and drums in the browser.

This is the culmination of months of work and hundreds of billions of frontier tokens. It all started when I wanted to see what Fable 5 could really do, so I thought of the most comically ambitious project I could think of: FrankenSim, the system that unifies ALL of physics into a single coherent and cohesive simulation across all domains: mechanics, fluid dynamics, electricity and magnetism, etc., instead of modeling each domain as a separate silo, where each domain can use the same generic geometric primitives, solvers, calculus machinery, etc.

All unified using the language of sheaf cohomology to maintain consistency between representations, and where everything is made as legible, intuitive, and ergonomic to AI agents as possible.

This music simulation stuff is just the beginning. Beyond many more instruments, I'm going to be using FrankenSim to model HVAC systems, fluid flow through plumbing systems, and more!

Build a single-file headless newsletter engine (`server.ts`) running on Bun + `bun:sqlite` (WAL mode) + AWS SES on a €4/mo Hetzner VPS. 0 external SaaS dependencies, 0 Admin UI, the entire control plane is a remote MCP server.

1. SQLite Schema (`db.sqlite`, WAL + busy_timeout):
- subscribers(id, email UNIQUE, status['pending'|'active'|'bounced'|'complained'|'unsubscribed'], tier['free'|'paid'], source, attrs JSON, token UNIQUE, created_at)
- posts(id, slug UNIQUE, title, mdx_free, mdx_paid, sent_at)
- send_queue(id, post_id, subscriber_id, subject, status['queued'|'sent'|'failed'], attempts, next_retry_at, UNIQUE(post_id, subscriber_id))
- events(id, subscriber_id, post_id, type['delivered'|'opened'|'clicked'|'bounced'|'complained'], meta JSON, ts)

2. Public HTTP Routes (`Bun.serve`):
- GET / & GET /p/:slug -> server-rendered HTML web archive + RSS feed at /rss.xml (unlock `mdx_paid` if signed cookie is paid)
- GET /media/:file -> serve optimized images directly from local `/var/data/media/`
- POST /subscribe -> rate-limit by IP in memory, reject disposable domains, upsert subscriber, send magic-link opt-in via SES
- GET /magic/:token -> activate subscriber + set HMAC signed session cookie, redirect to /
- POST /u/:token & GET /u/:token -> RFC 8058 1-click instant unsubscribe
- POST /webhooks/ses -> verify AWS SNS signature, process Bounce (Hard -> 'bounced', Soft -> ignore), Complaint (-> 'complained'), Delivery/Open/Click -> insert into `events`
- POST /webhooks/stripe -> verify signature, flip `tier = 'paid' | 'free'`

3. Background Worker + Email Compiler (in-process loop, 0 Redis/Inngest):
- Compile MDX to Outlook-safe table HTML via `react-email/render` and verify `Buffer.byteLength(html) < 102000` (Gmail 102KB clip limit).
- Every 1s, pull up to 50 due rows from `send_queue`, send concurrently via SES `SendEmail` with `List-Unsubscribe` + `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` headers, and exponential backoff on 429/5xx.

4. Remote MCP Server (`POST /mcp` with Bearer token):
- `sql_query(sql)`: read-only SQL over SQLite (replaces all analytics dashboards, cohort charts, and segment builders)
- `save_post(slug, title, mdx_free, mdx_paid)`: upsert draft, return Gmail byte-size check + web preview link
- `upload_media(filename, base64)`: resize/convert to WebP via `sharp`, save to disk, return URL
- `send_test(slug, to_email)`: send rendered preview email
- `send_post(slug, where_sql, ab_subjects?)`: populate `send_queue` for active subscribers matching `where_sql` (e.g. "tier = 'paid' AND json_extract(attrs, '$.topic') = 'ai'")
- `mutate_sql(sql, params)`: tag, import CSV, or update subscribers/automations directly

He's right that increasing your looks or status will make you more generally attractive as a man (obviously). But the rest is pretty blackpilled and overly online. What he's missing:

- There is no universal SMV. Even on looks, raters in our Keeper data disagree a lot about the same photo, and research on faces finds taste is half shared, half personal (Germine et al. 2015).
- The "money maxx" trophy wife trade is rarer than people think. Good-looking people pair with good-looking people, successful with successful, etc. Controlling for that erases most of the beauty-for-status exchange (McClintock 2014).
- Swipe apps and Instagram are efficient at one thing: sorting people on photos. Optimizing your perceived looks and status for that gets you to a local maximum. But what predicts whether a relationship actually works (kindness, emotional stability, how you two get along) is not efficiently matched at all on swipe apps. And 63% of single women who are looking haven't used a dating app in the past year (Pew).
- The longer people know each other, the less they agree on who's attractive. Among people who know each other well, personal taste beats consensus by a wide margin (Eastwick & Hunt 2014).
- Couples who started dating within a month of meeting were strongly looksmatched, while couples who knew each other 9+ months first were barely looksmatched - and just as happy (Hunt, Eastwick & Finkel 2015). That's why his own exceptions (college, grad school) work, and you can still do that after school you graduate with friend groups, work, church, and hobbies.

heres the whole outbound system we run, every step in order (steal it):

STEP 1: PICK A MARKET WORTH SENDING TO

- count your market in sales navigator account search
- 3,000 companies is the floor, 10,000+ is better
- each customer has to be worth $2k+ to you
- one ICP and one job title per campaign

a small market with a cheap product cant pay for outbound, no matter how good the copy is

STEP 2: BUILD AN OFFER A STRANGER CAN SAY YES TO

a cold buyer doesnt know you, so asking for 30 minutes is a big ask

lead with one of these:

- something free and useful to them
- a result from a company like theirs
- taking the risk away with a guarantee

pull your best case study numbers into one sheet before you write a word

STEP 3: BUILD THE COMPANY LIST FIRST

- run account search before lead search
- then pull the decision makers inside those companies
- use every variation of the job title
- split big searches city by city

sales nav stops at 2,500 results per search

15 cities turns one capped search into 37,500 people

then have AI read every company website and pass or fail it with a one line reason

the people who report your messages are the ones who never should have been on the list

STEP 4: GIVE EVERY LEAD A REASON TO HEAR FROM YOU TODAY

- changed jobs in the last 90 days
- promoted recently
- posted on linkedin in the last 30 days
- commenting on a competitors posts
- registered for an event in your space
- hiring for the role you replace
- raised a round

new in role leaders reply about 3x more for us

save every search and turn on alerts so new people land on your list automatically

STEP 5: SET UP THE LINKEDIN ACCOUNTS

- verified profiles that belong to real people
- clear photo, headline with the result you create
- 500+ connections and a few recent posts
- open profile switched on
- log in from the same place every time

warm each account for 3 to 4 weeks:

- week 1: connect, react, share one post
- week 2: more requests, normal chats
- week 3: a few cold messages
- week 4: hold a steady pace

keep a spare account warming in case one gets a warning

STEP 6: SET UP EMAIL

- never send cold email from your main domain
- 2 to 3 inboxes per domain (we use inboxkit)
- SPF, DKIM and DMARC on every domain
- warm every inbox for 2 weeks
- send from dedicated IPs (we use sendkit)
- verify every email before it goes in a sequence
- test inbox placement before every campaign

gmail made DMARC mandatory for bulk senders in feb 2024 and outlook followed in may 2025

skip this step and your copy never gets read

STEP 7: WRITE THE MESSAGE

- subject line is their first name, nothing else
- open with a result for a company like theirs
- end on one question they can say yes to
- ask for something small, "want the breakdown?"
- write 3 to 5 versions of every line

first name subjects have taken our inmails past 50% replies

the best cold message we ever sent was 19 words

if your first message has a calendly link and a deck in it, thats where your replies went

STEP 8: SEND ON LINKEDIN FIRST

- message open profiles first, no connection needed
- connection notes are one line with no pitch
- send a 30 second voice note after they accept
- message event attendees and group members directly
- spread sends across the day and do less at weekends

a reply inside 90 days refunds the inmail credit, even a no

and reply rate decides how much linkedin lets you send, so targeting protects your account

STEP 9: MOVE THE WINNER TO EMAIL

- test 2 offers on linkedin
- read the replies inside a day or two
- move the winning angle to email
- email the same people 3 days later

linkedin alone gets around 15% responses for us, email alone around 3%

both on the same people gets close to 35%

STEP 10: FOLLOW UP

- day 3 or 4: send another client result
- day 7 to 10: ask about their timing
- then stop and recycle them into a later campaign
- if your first contact goes quiet, message a colleague
- for hard to reach execs, message their chief of staff

a follow up that only says "just bumping this" gets ignored, every one needs a new reason

STEP 11: WORK THE REPLIES

- answer inside 5 minutes
- one person owns each reply
- call every interested reply before it books
- offer a specific time, "does tuesday at 11am work?"
- log every "come back in Q1" with the date
- turn every "wrong person" into an introduction

answered inside 5 minutes, 45% book a meeting

leave it to the next day and 3% do

STEP 12: TRACK IT EVERY WEEK

- connection acceptance, aim for 30%+
- reply rate by type of company
- interested replies
- meetings booked
- how fast replies get answered
- any warnings or restrictions

when a number drops:

- warnings or low acceptance: slow down
- low replies: change the list
- replies but no interest: change the result
- interest but no meetings: reply faster and call more

if an account gets a warning, rest it for 2 weeks and restart on your best leads

thats the whole system

You already gave the LLM the answer. So why is it writing it out from scratch?

Introducing a new AI model architecture: Constrained Decoding Models (CDMs)

LLMs were built to write. Most production workloads just need an answer: fast, consistent, and affordable.

CDMs are purpose-built for 1 task each. They read your input once and skip the token-by-token generative loop that makes LLMs slow and expensive.

Not just a decision model, but a family of 3 CDMs live today:

• Classify: define your labels and get back a calibrated probability + reason for each. Used for routing, tagging, and intent detection.
 • Extract: describe the entities in natural language and get back well-formed JSON with confidence scores + citations. Used for web scraping, document processing, and PII redaction.
 • Summarize: pass in long text, images, or PDFs and get back a consistent summary under 1,000 tokens. Used for context compaction, metadata generation, and transcript digests.

Built for production:

• 1M tokens of multimodal (text + image) input, 31x larger than Jev
 • 77.2% on DecisionBench vs Jev's 72%
 • 200x faster, 467x cheaper than frontier LLM APIs
 • $0.05/M input tokens. Output is free (yes, even for summarize)

Being good at your job and being good at interviewing for the next one are two different skills.  

The job rewards patience and judgment over months. Meanwhile, the interview rewards clear stories told in a few minutes each.  

If you're employed and looking:

- Keep a private log of your projects and wins while the details are fresh.
- Turn your best ones into short stories with STAR: the situation, the task, what you did, and the result.
- Practice technical rounds and whiteboarding out loud, so you can explain your thought process as you go.
- Ask the recruiter for the exact interview format before you prep.
- Ask the interviewer what problems the team is dealing with, then show how you'd fix one using a real example from your work.

Nobody on the panel has seen your track record, you have to provide the context and tell it.

Small RL companies are the AI industry's equivalent of quant shops. Let me explain.

Both are small, secretive, full of brilliant people, profitable, and always one step from their edge disappearing.

The parallels:

- Secretive. Nobody publishes their signals. Labs won't say what they're training next, and vendors can't say who they sell to. Epoch calls the market "largely behind closed doors."

- Hunting alpha. For a quant, a trade stops working once everyone finds it. For these shops, a task stops paying once models can solve it (labs drop tasks at around 70% pass rate). Meanwhile, labs are building their own in-house. So they always have to find the next field.

- Deep Industry Connections. You need to know the problem cold to get in. Founders have usually worked at, or sold to, the labs. You can't define "correct" for fund accounting without having done fund accounting.

- They buy strange data. Quants buy satellite photos of parking lots. RL shops bid for enterprise data (eg $12.5M bid for Spirit Airlines historical data).

- Brilliant people. Quants hire math olympiad winners. These shops hire ex-lab researchers and real practitioners.

- Huge revenue per head. Jane Street made about $11M per employee in 2025. Proximal is about $5M. The tweet's company would be $20M.

- One narrow problem that makes something more efficient. Quants make markets more efficient. These RL shops make models training more efficient.

- High risk (for different reasons). A quant can lose millions in a day on a bad trade. An RL shop's risk is that one lab trains a model that makes their environments irrelevant, or brings the work in-house, and the revenue stops.

- Overfitting/reward hacking. A quant's nightmare is a strategy that looks perfect on historical data and fails live. An RL shop's nightmare is an RL grader that scores perfectly and trains the model incorrectly. 

- Infrastructure arms race. Quants pay for microseconds of speed. RL shops race to spin up thousands of disposable computers per training run.

Obviously there are as many differences between RL companies and quant shops, but right now the aura around them feels eerily similar. 

Curious to see how this market matures as robotics opens up a new surface, and whether the frontier labs end up absorbing them.

As CEO of Product Hunt, I see hundreds of launches a week. One trait separates winners from losers.

Every few months, new models come out. Some products become better, effortlessly. Some don't improve, or become irrelevant.

This property needs a name. I'm calling it Buoyancy.

Buoyant startups rise with model improvements the way a boat rises with the tide. 

Anti-buoyant startups come in two flavors: over-scaffolded (which hinders the new, smarter models) and too thin - which makes them redundant when models improve. 

To be buoyant, you need a "hull" - usually proprietary data, a vertical-specific harness, network effects, or distribution advantage. This hull keeps you buoyant as models improve. 

Hulls are the new moats.

My number one advice to startups in 2026: Be buoyant. Find your hull. 

(Full essay on my blog)

The creative system you should run depending on your monthly Meta spend:

1/ Under $25K a month

You can't afford to shoot your way to a winner at this size, so don't try.

Copy what already works. Open your competitors' longest-running ads and rebuild the format for your product.

Statics carry this tier. Three of our strategists made 20 to 30 statics in about an hour and found winners, and some of them became top spenders.

A winner here has to take real spend. A ROAS 4 ad that spent $50 isn't one.

2/ $25K to $100K a month

This is where volume starts.

10 concepts a month, 5 hooks on each, plus iterations on whatever wins. That's 65 ads, and it's the minimum we ship for any client.

Every concept has to be completely different from the others, because under Andromeda similar ads get the same entity ID and fight over the same people.

Usually 1 of 3 hooks wins, so you only need one to carry the concept.

Hook rate is the leading indicator. Our app client's best old ad sat at 25%, so we put a hook from a 58% ad in front of it.

That account went from $6K in ad spend in April to $392K in July on about 100 ads a month, with the funnel, pricing and LTV untouched.

3/ $100K to $1M a month

The explanation formats take over here, podcast especially when the product needs explaining.

One podcast client spent $180K at a $67 CPA in week one. By week three it was $400K at $48.

5 to 10 new concepts a week, each one a different format, persona or awareness level.

Stop judging single ads and look at when your last true winner launched. If it's 3+ months old, that's the problem.

4/ $1M+ a month

This is pure volume with intent behind every ad. Two of the accounts we run sit at 4,800 and 12,000 ads.

Set weekly input targets for concepts, ads, landing pages and one LTV test every week or two, and give every target an owner.

Find the tier you're in today and run that system before you copy the next tier up.

I don’t ask clients what they want automated. They don’t know.

I ask them to walk me through their week. Then I listen for three things.

One. Anything they do the exact same way every time, like onboarding, invoices, reporting or follow-ups. Repetition is money.

Two. Anything where a person copies info from one place to another. Emails into the CRM, PDFs into a spreadsheet. That’s pure gold.

Three. Anything they say “we should really sort that out” about. They’ve already decided it’s worth fixing, you just have to offer.

Then I do the maths out loud.

“You said someone spends an hour a day on this. That’s 5 hours a week, about 260 hours a year. That’s over 6 weeks of someone’s wages spent copying and pasting.”

Now the price makes sense before I’ve even said a number.

That one conversation is usually where the $5k automation is hiding.

I’m not selling n8n or Zapier workflows. I’m selling those 6 weeks back.

The tools are the easy part. Understanding the problem and showing what it costs to leave it is what gets you paid.

The main fix is the maths. An hour a day is about 260 hours a year, which is closer to six and a half working weeks than “a full month”. Someone in the replies will check, so it’s better to have the right number. It’s also bigger, which makes the point stronger.

if nobody's posting about it (or the only views come from massive accounts) demand is unproven. you'd be gambling that people care about something the market hasn't validated yet

this doesn't mean you need to copy what exists. it means you need to confirm that the underlying desire is real before investing time into building content around it

Fork-and-Flush: help your agents escape Idea Basins!!

I love thinking of AutoResearch as Idea Descent: a metric of interest goes down, as a function of ideas/experiments, where the agents get pulled towards one idea or another. But we've seen very often an agent develop this weird tunnel vision, and honing in just one type of "idea", kinda like GD stuck in a local minimum. 

We studied this and seems we can fix it with Fork-and-Flush, a super simple and kinda cute idea. Every so often, fork the agent into T copies in the same workspace but empty the context, let them run for a bit, and continue from the best one. 

If you like the GD analogy, it's basically basin hopping https://t.co/NOzpRGT3It.

BTW we found a silly way of also plotting "idea basins": an LLM rewrites every experiment as a spec and answers a few thousand binary queries "is Experiment A closer to B or to C?". Then we embed this NXN matrix into 2D and indeed see in many cases that each run saturates into a small region and keeps polishing it. 

We call these idea basins!

At equal compute Fork and Flush beats single runs and best-of-N on 12/13 long-horizon tasks (some 4+ days), and in my own research projects it's been working really well! 

BTW we only use it at test time, but it could also be part of training or RL.

Now the less obvious:

We are witnessing something similar to the internet boom, where a hyper verticalized society (one person talks to millions, through the TV news) became a hyper horizontalized society (millions of people talking to each other), but most of the value ended up captured by a handful of platforms (facebook, google etc), that all of them were talking through.

This time millions of people, (non programmers included), are able to build through code, and once again, most of them are doing it through the same 3/4 models.

It looks diverse from the outside, but it’s actually very fragile because all of it depends on the same base.

In 1938, Brazil started banning the German language in Blumenau.

Today that same city throws the biggest German festival in the Americas.

German settlers founded Blumenau in 1850, in Santa Catarina, in the south of Brazil.

For generations, families there spoke German at home, at school and in their newspapers.

Then President Getúlio Vargas launched a campaign to make everyone in Brazil speak only Portuguese.

German schools were closed, German newspapers stopped printing, and families were banned from speaking the language, even at home.

Many parents stopped teaching their children the language their grandparents brought across the ocean.

In the 1970s, city leaders started planning a festival to bring that heritage back into the open.

Then the Itajaí-Açu River flooded the city four times in 1983.

On August 7th, 1984, the river rose to 15.46 meters, more than 50 feet.

Many people think the festival was invented to cheer the city up after the floods, but the plan was already on the table.

Two months after that flood, on October 5th, 1984, the first Oktoberfest opened anyway, and 102,000 people walked in.

By 1988, more than 1 million people came in a single year.

Last year, 689,201 people came, and the festival handed the city a record R$12 million profit.

This year's edition runs October 7th to 25th, with a parade tomorrow morning for the October 12th holiday.

Brazil once tried to silence German in Blumenau, and the city answered by turning it into the party that fills its streets every October. https://t.co/CuuSkCilJY

TLDR Ultimately, housing prices reflect more than the cost of construction. They reflect land administration, infrastructure, economic concentration, supply constraints, and the availability of alternative investment assets.

Long version 
The cost of housing in Nigeria goes beyond design. I can't stand the soulless architecture of many so called luxury homes here, but I understand that a lot more goes into property pricing than the quality of the building itself.

Consider location, access to infrastructure, security, and proximity to business districts.

Few Nigerian cities have the economic pull of Lagos. Even within Lagos, the number of locations with decent infrastructure, security, and convenient access to business districts is limited relative to demand.

Then there's our suboptimal land administration system, where obtaining properly titled land can be an incredibly difficult process.

All of this is compounded by the limited investment options available to Nigerians. Housing isn't just accommodation; it's also an investment asset. Property prices are driven not only by the need for shelter but also by investors looking to preserve and grow their wealth.

These factors contribute to the insane property valuations we see in Nigeria's major cities.

This is why blindly comparing Nigerian property prices with those in South Africa or the US misses the bigger picture.

Yes, American homes are generally better built, with better infrastructure and more reliable public services. But the US also has a much larger number of locations with good infrastructure and economic opportunities, giving people more options and creating competition that helps moderate prices.

There's also a much deeper and more accessible investment market in the US. People can invest in the S&P 500, bonds, and other financial instruments instead of relying so heavily on real estate to preserve their wealth.

When people have more viable investment options, less capital is forced into property.

Ultimately, housing prices reflect more than the cost of construction. They reflect land administration, infrastructure, economic concentration, supply constraints, and the availability of alternative investment assets.

Until we address these underlying issues, comparing property prices across countries without considering their different economic realities will always be an incomplete argument.

Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

In 1975, Steve Jobs told Steve Wozniak that Atari had paid them $700 for a game they built together. He handed Woz a check for $350.

Atari had actually paid Jobs about $5,000.

In the video below, Woz says: "Who cares about money? Well, you do care about friendship and honesty."

Jobs was working the night shift at Atari. The company wanted a new arcade game called Breakout, built with as few chips as possible.

Jobs couldn't build it. Woz could. He already had a full-time job at Hewlett-Packard, and Jobs said they had four days. Woz went four days with no sleep. Both of them came down with mono.

Woz did it in 45 chips. Atari's own engineers were using 150 or more.

He took his $350 and was happy with it. Jobs took the rest and went up to Oregon to buy into a farm.

About ten years later, Woz read the real number in a book about Atari. By then the two of them had built Apple, and Woz was a multimillionaire.

If Jobs had just told him he needed the money, Woz says, "I would say take it all."

It wasn't the last time. Before Apple went public in 1980, Jobs refused to give stock options to Daniel Kottke, his friend since college, who had helped build the first Apple computers.

Woz did the opposite. He sold his own shares cheaply to Kottke and other early employees who had been left out.

One friend kept almost all of a $5,000 bonus. The other gave away millions.

Was Jobs a genius who knew what business takes, or just a bad friend?

The problem with running a small business is that you can’t experiment (because you have no money), you don’t know how to build companies properly, and you’ve never seen from the inside how successful businesses actually grow.

So you start believing everything you see on X:

- that founder content drives sales (rather than cold outreach on LinkedIn).
- that UGC videos made with a phone and a VPN can make you $100k/month (rather than paid ads or boring SEO).
- that one-off feature launch videos with millions of views and PR generate sales (when their real long-term goal is to attract investors, partners, and employees).

And so on.

You can learn all of this either by working for a company (ideally on the business side, in marketing or operations) or by spending VC money.

Everything else is a very long road that often leads to making very little money.

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

This app hit #1 on the US App Store

It's a consumer social app

And here's the viral UGC format behind their success

The viral format → someone gets a text from their crush and starts typing a reply that’s way too eager. Then Bro, an orange cartoon character that sits on top of their phone screen, jumps in, tells them to play it cool, and writes a better reply

> you’re watching a little dating drama, and by the end you’ve also seen exactly what the app does

Here's the 4-step structure every top video follows:
1. Start with a small moment that feels huge, like a text from your crush, a date who cancels, or not knowing which photo to post

2. Bro pops up on top of the app you’re already using, so it’s clear it sees what you see

3. Bro reacts in its blunt, funny voice, like stopping you right before you send a bad text

4. You follow Bro’s advice, and the video shows how it turns out

Why it works:
1. People stay for the story, they want to know what happened

2. The videos don't mention AI. They show Bro helping in one stressful moment, like when you have no idea what to text back - and that’s way easier to relate to

3. The orange character makes Bro easy to spot. Even when nobody says the app’s name, you know whose video it is

4. Bro shows up right where you’re making the choice, on top of apps like Instagram, so you see it help in real time

The format has 3 variations worth knowing:
1/ Dating and texting
This is the strongest one. Almost everyone has stressed over a text from a crush, so viewers get the problem in a second and stay to see what happens. In one video, a crush cancels plans, and Bro comments like a friend would

2/ Everyday decisions
Here Bro helps with small choices inside other apps. In one post, it sits on top of DoorDash, guesses the calories, and comments on the dessert. In another, it picks which photo to post on Instagram and writes the caption

3/ Motivation
In these videos, the app shows up on the phone’s lock screen to push someone who doesn’t feel like working out or doing homework. You can see what the app does, but there’s no real story in there

Key takeaways for marketers:
1, Put your app inside a story people already care about
2. Talk about the problem, and keep the app in the background
3. Show your app helping in the first few seconds
4. Give your app a look people can spot in one second, like Bro’s orange character
5. Pick one main promise and tie every feature back to it
6. End every video by showing the app name and what to search
7. Switch up the story, the setting, and the creator from video to video. When every post is the same phone close-up, the accounts start to feel fake

I've finally invested in enough unicorns (at seed) that I have confidence in the traits unicorn founders have in common.

If you fail to hone these traits, you will fail to build a $1B+ company in my experience.

/ 1. Velocity consists of speed

Matt Loszak from Aalo showed me this the most: The best founders are viscerally uncomfortable with slow progress.

They feel it as a physical irritant, not an abstract concern.

They obsessively refactor how they’re pursuing goals to identify clever shortcuts and rethink their roadmap from first principles.

Speed leads to high momentum and a compounding returns on knowledge and product. 

It’s necessary to maintain your headstart in a market, otherwise the faster competitor will beat you within a couple years.

/ 2. Velocity consists of direction

The best founders regularly surface from heads-down execution to ask whether their path is still the right one — whether a better route to the destination has opened up, or whether the destination itself has shifted.

Pathfinding prevents the common failure mode of executing brilliantly in the wrong direction.

It requires intellectual honesty and the willingness to kill plans that no longer make sense.

The best founders set a recurring quarterly calendar event to re-assess all their goals.

/ 3. Mission alignment

The journey to building a unicorn is long.

Without a mission that goes beyond financial outcome, most founders lose steam and start phoning it in. Then they get surpassed by competitors who are hungrier.

The mission doesn't have to be world-saving — but it has to be genuine to you.

/ 4. Asking for advice and integrating it

The best founders ask smart people for advice and implement the good advice immediately. The moment they’re shown a better way, they update their processes.

They don’t assume they’ll stumble into better ways organically; they set aside time each week to learn from others and shortcut their development. 

They assemble a counsel of advisors who are the best in the world at what they do and they sell them on the mission.

/ 5. Brick-by-brick hiring

Adam Guild of Owner showed me this the most.

Unicorn founders treat each early hire as weight-bearing. They run a deliberate process to find the best person in the world for each role — not whoever is closest at hand ("hiring within arm's reach") from their existing networks. (Unless they are the best). 

The foundation built in the first ten hires sets the ceiling for everything that follows. A single mis-hire in a key seat early on compounds. Getting this right means the team itself becomes a competitive moat.

You can’t run from the grind. I see a lot of 40+ professionals that don’t have the energy and mental stamina to make through the second half of their careers. The demand is higher than it’s ever been plan accordingly.

Check sizes and quality of the founders.

there’s a particular kind of 30-year-old guy who is still psychologically living in the best year of his life.
he had something happen at 24.
a startup took off. a job paid absurdly well. an investment worked. someone important noticed him. for about eleven months, the future looked completely obvious.
he was going to be somebody.
then the thing stopped working.
six years later, he’s still negotiating with the version of himself who thought he had already figured life out.

i think early success can do something genuinely cruel to a person if it arrives before they’ve learned how to be ordinary.
it teaches you to associate your identity with acceleration.
you’re the promising one.
the guy who figured it out young.
the one relatives ask about at thanksgiving because apparently something exciting is always happening with you.
until it isn't.

now you're 31, your income is inconsistent, your friends are buying houses, and you're explaining another business idea to your parents over dinner.
your dad asks whether you've considered getting a regular job.
you hear it as a request to identify the exact moment your life went wrong.

the complicated part is that you probably could get a decent job.
you have a degree. you know how to speak professionally. you have contacts. you understand enough corporate language to survive a meeting about absolutely nothing.
but somewhere along the way, a normal salary became psychologically associated with surrender.

you spent so many years imagining yourself escaping the system that participating in it now feels humiliating.
meanwhile the person who accepted a boring job at 25 has been promoted twice, developed useful relationships, saved money, and learned how to operate inside an actual organization.
you have seventeen tabs open about starting an AI company.
one of them is a youtube video called "why 2026 will create more millionaires than ever."
it's 1:38 am.

this is the part i find genuinely sad.
sometimes family money gives people just enough protection from consequences to keep an identity crisis running for years.
there's no spectacular collapse.
just a long, quiet decline in options.
the ambition stays enormous while the evidence gets smaller.
you start avoiding old friends because their perfectly normal questions require increasingly elaborate answers.
"what are you working on these days?"
god.

you used to love that question.
eventually you become more committed to preserving the possibility of an extraordinary future than doing the fairly unimpressive things that might actually produce one.

and nobody wants to talk about how addictive potential can be.
potential is wonderful because it never has to submit quarterly results.
you can be brilliant in theory for decades.

you can keep insisting that you're one connection, one opportunity, one launch away.
the really painful possibility is that your first success was real, your ambition is real, and you still have to start again at the bottom of something.
at 31.

with people younger than you.
without making a speech about how you used to be ahead.
some guys would genuinely rather spend another five years being a future millionaire than spend six months being a beginner.
and the worst part is they know exactly what they're doing.

they just can't bear to have anyone watch them start over.

This is way more common than you think. If you hit it big late 20s/early 30s, we always say "don't change your lifestyle for a year"

There is always a chance it's your biggest win. In addition, if you keep the dopamine in check, lady luck shows up later. If you don't she's gone

having an opinion creates engagement from people who agree AND people who disagree. both reactions carry equal weight in the algorithm

"slideshows outperform videos for app marketing" is polarizing because video creators will disagree. it's not offensive, just a position backed by data

a post everyone agrees with generates likes

T-Mobile spent five years trying to get rid of the exact spectrum Elon just called "the last critical piece" of complete phone coverage in America.

This 800 MHz block is Sprint's old Nextel spectrum, the stuff that powered push-to-talk walkie-talkie phones in 2004. The DOJ forced T-Mobile to divest it as a condition of the $26 billion Sprint merger. Dish had first rights at $3.59 billion and walked away because it couldn't raise the money. T-Mobile finally offloaded it to an investment firm called Grain Management last year for $2.9 billion plus a spectrum swap.

Grain's original plan was selling it to utilities for private networks.

Fourteen months later, SpaceX buys the whole portfolio, and shares of the carriers who passed on it fall as much as 8% in a single afternoon.

Here's why it matters so much. Starlink's satellite signal at 2 GHz can reach your phone outdoors, but it dies at the first wall. 800 MHz penetrates buildings. Most phones already have the band built in. So satellites handle the open sky, this low-band layer handles indoors, and suddenly Starlink Mobile covers everywhere a normal carrier does without the tower network.

Stack the moves. $17 billion for EchoStar's 50 MHz of 2 GHz spectrum. FCC approval for 15,000 Gen2 satellites this week. Now the low-band coverage layer.

Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile paid $81 billion in a single auction for C-band spectrum in 2021, then spent years and tens of billions more deploying it on towers. SpaceX assembled a nationwide carrier out of a distressed-asset sale, a forced divestiture castoff, and rockets it already owns.

The walkie-talkie spectrum from 2004 ended up being the piece that lets satellites replace cell towers. Nobody who touched it for twenty years saw that coming.

Chinese factories are buying RTX 5090s in bulk, desoldering the chips, and rebuilding them as 128GB server cards. Roughly $4,000 each.

Same money as a DGX Spark. Same 128GB. Six times the bandwidth.

The reason this exists: export controls block Chinese labs from buying dedicated AI chips, so consumer gaming cards became the workaround. Rip the GPU and memory off the board, solder onto a custom server PCB, add a blower cooler so it fits a rack instead of a gaming case. Automated soldering lines, robotic arms. Started with the 5090, now spreading to the 5080, 5070 Ti, 5060 Ti.

NVIDIA gets paid either way. They just lost control of what happens after the sale.

Two things follow from this:

Gamers are the collateral. Consumer cards are being bought in volume and stripped for AI, which is part of why you can't get one at a sane price.

And the "$4,000 for 128GB" pitch that DGX and Strix Halo are built on now has a grey-market competitor with dramatically better bandwidth — assuming you can get one, trust the soldering, and live without support.

A lot of smart advice came in

Here are the key takeaways people highlighted:

• Latency is everything
REST is too slow. WebSockets, servers as close as possible to Polymarket, and measuring ping down to milliseconds really matter

• Speed > logic
Arbitrage dies in the gap between price detection and order execution

• Language & infra matter
Python can work, but many recommend Rust or C++ with optimized RPC. 

Looks like I'll have to try Rust🧠

• Batch orders & order types
Sending multiple orders in one request and using the right order types can save critical time

• Security basics
Don't store private keys in plain files - use proper key management
